gifford1979.title: Weighted Voting for Replicated Data
gifford1979.author: David K. Gifford
gifford1979.venue: Proceedings of the Seventh ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '79), pp. 150-162
gifford1979.quote: In a new algorithm for maintaining replicated data, every copy of a replicated file is assigned some number of votes. Every transaction collects a read quorum of r votes to read a file, and a write quorum of w votes to write a file, such that r + w is greater than the total number of votes assigned to the file. This ensures that there is a non-null intersection between every read quorum and every write quorum. Version numbers make it possible to determine which copies are current.
supports: r + w greater than the total number of votes assigned to the file
non-null intersection between every read quorum and every write quorum
version numbers determine which copies are current
byline on the published paper reads 'Stanford University and Xerox Palo Alto Research Center'

gifford1979tr.title: Weighted Voting for Replicated Data (Xerox PARC technical report CSL-79-14)
gifford1979tr.author: David K. Gifford
gifford1979tr.venue: Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, Computer Science Laboratory
gifford1979tr.quote: David Gifford is a graduate student at Stanford University, and this work was supported in part by the Xerox Corporation and by the Fannie and John Hertz Foundation. This paper was presented at the Seventh Symposium on Operating System Principles on December 12, 1979 in Pacific Grove, California.
supports: Gifford was a Stanford graduate student, not a PARC staff researcher
report number CSL-79-14, dated September 1979 on the title page
the SOSP talk was given on 12 December 1979 at Pacific Grove, California

section 4.1: 'We can incorporate temporary copies into the algorithm by introducing representatives with no votes, called weak representatives. Such a representative will not change the quorums of a file suite, and thus can be introduced at any time. However, it can be included in any quorum' - a weak representative is readable inside a quorum; what it never does is change the quorum arithmetic

dynamo2007.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
dynamo2007.author: Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani, Gunavardhan Kakulapati, Avinash Lakshman, Alex Pilchin, Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, Peter Vosshall, Werner Vogels
dynamo2007.quote: Setting R and W such that R + W > N yields a quorum-like system. In this model, the latency of a get (or put) operation is dictated by the slowest of the R (or W) replicas. For this reason, R and W are usually configured to be less than N, to provide better latency.
supports: R + W > N as the tunable-consistency knob in Dynamo's descendants

the sloppy quorum relaxation: 'it does not enforce strict quorum membership and instead it uses a “sloppy quorum”; all read and write operations are performed on the first N healthy nodes from the preference list, which may not always be the first N nodes encountered while walking the consistent hashing ring.'
Dynamo's reference [22] is Thomas' majority-consensus paper; the Dynamo paper does not cite Gifford

gifford1979related.title: Weighted Voting for Replicated Data, section 2 (Related Work)
gifford1979related.author: David K. Gifford
gifford1979related.quote: Thomas' proposal [11] only requires that a majority of an object's copies be updated, and includes voting.
supports: the prior published rule was majority-of-copies, and it already included voting
'Thomas' algorithm does not employ weighted voters, which limits its flexibility.'
'We do not insist that a majority of an object's copies be updated.'
Gifford's reference [11] is: Thomas, R.H. A Majority Consensus Approach to Concurrency Control for Multiple Copy Databases, ACM Trans. on Database Systems 4, 2 (June 1979), pp. 180-209.

unverified: Robert H. Thomas, 'A Majority Consensus Approach to Concurrency Control for Multiple Copy Databases', ACM TODS 4(2), June 1979, pp. 180-209 — confirmed only as reference [11] in Gifford's own bibliography and reference [22] in the Dynamo paper. The ACM full text returned HTTP 403 and the paper itself was never opened, so nothing from Thomas appears in the prose.

Any direct line of descent from Gifford's 1979 paper to Dynamo. Dynamo states R + W > N but cites Thomas, not Gifford; the connection drawn on the ripple card is between the two published formulations, not a documented influence.
What Violet's replication cost in money. The paper reports latency, message counts and blocking probabilities and no budget figure; no currency amount is claimed anywhere in this story.
